prompt: Write an essay titled “The Elasticity Business”. It is about elasticity of supply and demand over different timescales, and about businesses that profit from supplying capacity when it is scarce. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
Ask an economist how much the price of something will change when demand rises, and the honest answer is "it depends on when you ask." In the first hour, almost nothing can adjust. In the first month, some things can. Over a decade, nearly everything can. The same market that looks brutally rigid on Tuesday looks soft and accommodating over a generation. This gap between short-run and long-run elasticity is one of the most important facts in economics, and a surprising number of businesses exist to exploit it.

Consider oil. When a supply shock hits, drivers still have to get to work, factories still have to run, and planes still have to fly. Nobody can trade in their car for a more efficient one overnight, and no new well comes online in a week. Short-run demand and supply are both stubbornly inelastic, so a small shortage produces an enormous price spike. Give it five years, though, and people buy smaller cars, move closer to work, and insulate their homes, while producers drill in places that were uneconomical at the old price. The spike that looked permanent turns out to have contained the seeds of its own collapse. High prices are the cure for high prices, as traders like to say, but the cure takes time to work.

That delay is where the money is. If you can supply something during the window when nobody else can, you collect the difference between the short-run price and the long-run price. Electricity markets make this unusually vivid. Power must be produced the instant it is consumed, and on the hottest afternoon of the year demand can exceed what the regular fleet of plants can deliver. Grid operators then turn to "peaker" plants, gas turbines that sit idle for most of the year and run only a few dozen or a few hundred hours. Their economics look absurd on paper: enormous capital tied up in machines that do nothing almost all the time. But during those few hours, when wholesale prices can rise a hundredfold, a peaker can earn most of its annual revenue in an afternoon. Its owner isn't really in the electricity business. It's in the elasticity business.

The same pattern shows up everywhere once you look for it. Shipping companies that own vessels outright made fortunes in 2021, when pandemic disruption sent container rates up roughly tenfold and it takes years to build a new ship. Oil traders charter tankers and fill them with crude when the futures curve makes storage profitable, turning floating steel into a bet on time. Equipment rental firms keep fleets of generators and pumps ready for hurricane season. Cloud providers hold spare servers so that a customer whose traffic suddenly explodes can buy capacity in minutes rather than waiting months for hardware, and in the scramble for AI compute even a modest stock of available GPUs became valuable. Ride-hailing surge pricing is the consumer version: it pays drivers to show up exactly when the short-run supply curve is steepest.

What these businesses sell, at bottom, is an option. They pay to hold capacity that may never be used, and in exchange they get the right to supply it when it is most valuable. Like any option seller, they live with long stretches of quiet and the occasional enormous payoff. This makes them strange to evaluate. A peaker plant in a mild year looks like a failing business; a shipping line in 2019 looked like a commodity operation with thin margins. Judging them on any single year misses the point, because the bad years are the premium they pay and the crisis years are the claim that pays out.

It also makes them politically awkward. The moment they earn their money is precisely the moment everyone else is suffering. Prices that clear a market in a heat wave or a hurricane look, from the outside, like gouging. Sometimes they are. But the windfall is also the signal that justified holding the capacity in the first place. Cap the price during scarcity and you don't just prevent profiteering; you remove the reason anyone would keep spare turbines, spare generators, or spare ships around. Texas learned a version of this in the February 2021 freeze, when the grid's design and the incentives around winterization left too little capacity standing ready, and the costs of the shortfall vastly exceeded the costs of the preparation would have been.

There is a final irony. Every successful elasticity business invites the long-run response that destroys its margins. High charter rates trigger a wave of shipbuilding orders, and three years later the new vessels arrive into a glutted market. Profitable peakers attract batteries, which can respond even faster and charge cheaply when prices are low. Today's scarcity is tomorrow's overcapacity, and the firms that thrive across cycles are the ones that remember this when everyone else is extrapolating.

The deepest lesson is that scarcity is rarely a fixed fact about the world. It is a fact about the world over a particular horizon. Most people experience markets one moment at a time and are surprised by the volatility. The businesses that profit are the ones that understand which horizon they are standing in, hold the right capacity for the moments when nobody else can respond, and stay patient enough to be there when those moments come.
